analysis.one_liner: Requires brokers serving employer health plans to disclose hidden compensation from pharmacy benefit managers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 4, 2025 by one Republican and one Democratic senator, referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and has had no vote or further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends an existing pension-and-benefits disclosure law so that consultants and brokers who help employers run their health plans must reveal any direct or hidden payments they get from pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices — and from companies that administer claims. The point is to let employers see when their own advisor is being paid by the PBM it recommends, so they can negotiate better drug coverage deals. The Labor Department would have 180 days to write the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees covered by employer-sponsored health plans, and the employers who pay for those plans. When a broker's advice is quietly steered by payments from a PBM, employers may sign up for deals that look good on paper but hide fees and inflated drug costs. Forced disclosure of that compensation gives employers leverage to cut those costs, which flows back to workers in the form of lower premiums and out-of-pocket spending. The Labor Department also gains a clearer mandate to enforce the disclosure rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and employers with job-based health plans

how_it_helps.text: Adds pharmacy benefit management services and third-party administration services to the compensation that covered service providers must disclose to employer health plans, explicitly including indirect compensation — the hidden payments PBMs and their partners make to brokers and consultants.

Requires the Secretary of Labor to issue clarifying regulations within 180 days of enactment, applying to plan years beginning at least 6 months after the rules are issued, so the requirement takes practical effect rather than sitting as ambiguous statutory language.

By exposing conflicts of interest — for example, a broker recommending a PBM that pays the broker a fee — it gives employers the information they need to negotiate lower drug benefit costs, which is where workers' premium dollars go.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs, third-party administrators, and the benefits brokers and consultants who serve employer plans would bear the cost of disclosing and documenting their compensation arrangements. Firms whose business model depends on compensation that is not visible to plan sponsors would face the most pressure, and any revenue they lose from exposed fee arrangements comes out of arrangements that currently add cost to employer plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBMs and benefits brokers and consultants

drawbacks.text: Disclosure alone does not fix the underlying problem. The bill does not ban spread pricing, does not force PBMs to pass rebates to plans, and does not cap drug costs. An employer can be handed a technically complete disclosure buried in a long document and still fail to act on it.

The bill's own 'sense of Congress' section states that the amendment merely clarifies requirements that were already in effect since the No Surprises Act's application date, and imposes no additional requirement — so supporters are implicitly conceding the practical change may be small, and the measure functions partly as a congressional statement that the old rules already applied.

The burden falls on service providers and their subcontractors to track and report compensation across affiliated entities, which imposes real compliance and documentation costs on smaller firms in the benefits industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a low-cost, modest-reach transparency bill. For workers and employers it makes a genuine but indirect difference: it targets one specific channel — broker conflicts and hidden PBM compensation — through which drug benefit costs get inflated, without touching the larger PBM practices that drive prices. For PBMs and brokers, the cost is exposure of fee arrangements they currently keep out of sight. The honest criticism is that disclosure is the weakest tool available; if employers don't read or act on the disclosures, costs won't move. The bill is hard to oppose on the merits and limited in what it delivers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early December 2025, read twice, and sent to the Senate health committee, where it has sat with no markup, vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the PBM Disclosure Act in the Senate on December 4, 2025, joined by Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, giving it one Republican and one Democratic sponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which is its only action so far.
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action has been recorded since the referral, and the current Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet, in either direction. The bill is too new and too inactive for anyone to have won anything; PBMs and brokers keep their current arrangements for now simply because nothing has changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No decision yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PBM Disclosure Act on December 4, 2025.

for.name: Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor but no votes have occurred, so no partisan split is on the record; no opponents have acted on it publicly.

industries.note: The bill requires disclosure of direct and indirect compensation tied to PBM services sold to employer plans. PBMs profit from complex, hard-to-audit fee and rebate structures; forcing those arrangements into the open, even as a 'clarification', threatens deals that currently add cost to employer drug plans.

Many brokers receive compensation from the PBMs and vendors they recommend. The bill puts those payments on the disclosure requirement, exposing potential conflicts between the broker's advice and the employer's interests.

TPAs that process claims for self-insured employer plans are swept into the same disclosure requirement, and their related fees must be reported alongside PBM compensation. Compliance costs rise, but the largest TPAs are owned by the same insurance-PBM giants already affected.
Plan sponsors get a clearer statutory right to see every dollar their advisors and PBMs take, including indirect compensation, which strengthens their hand in fee negotiations.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills referred to committee never get a vote, and this one is only weeks old with a two-sponsor base. Its best realistic path is being folded into a larger PBM or health-cost package, since PBM reform has been an active topic on Capitol Hill; on its own, the likely outcome is that it sits in the HELP Committee and quietly dies at the end of the Congress unless leadership takes an interest.
